## Problem

The organization Project "Waaseyaa Framework" says it tracks all open waaseyaa/framework issues by milestone and priority. On 2026-08-29 it contained 74 items, all marked Done, while the repository had a large live open backlog and none of those current issues appeared on the board.

The older personal "Waaseyaa" Project is also historical/all-Done, but this issue concerns the organization board whose description claims current authority.

## Outcome

The Project is either a trustworthy current roadmap surface or is clearly marked historical/retired. It must not silently compete with issue labels and milestones.

## Acceptance

- Decide and document whether issues/milestones or Project fields are the canonical priority authority.
- If retained, synchronize every open framework issue and map Status/Priority deterministically from governed metadata.
- Detect sync drift automatically and prove new/closed issue behavior.
- Enforce the beta-gate invariant in the authoritative-to-mirror direction: every open issue labelled `release:beta-blocker` must have Project `Roadmap Stage = 0 - Safety`.
- Preserve the intentional non-equivalence in the reverse direction: a Stage-0 issue is not necessarily a beta blocker, and synchronization must never infer or add `release:beta-blocker` solely from Stage 0.
- Test both directions explicitly: fail when `release:beta-blocker` is outside Stage 0; allow Stage-0 issues without `release:beta-blocker`.
- If retired, update the description and archive/redirect it explicitly.
- Preserve issue history and avoid bulk field rewrites without a reviewed mapping.

## Non-goals

This issue does not change product priorities, release anything, or block #2653.


## Synchronization contract: the four axes are independent (added 2026-09-03)

Agents and reviewers keep rediscovering this and getting it wrong, most recently by treating
Roadmap Stage as a proxy for beta-gate membership. The synchronization this issue defines must
state the axes explicitly and must not derive any one of them from another.

| axis | carried by | means | does **not** mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gate membership** | `release:beta-blocker` label, and ultimately `support/beta-gate-v1.json` (#2860) | this issue must be remediated or explicitly excluded before beta | anything about when it is scheduled |
| **Readiness** | `status:*` labels (canonical); Project `Readiness` field mirrors them | whether it is actionable now | anything about which release claims it |
| **Delivery lane** | milestone -- one per issue | which workstream ships it | a release threshold; re-milestoning to a threshold erases the lane |
| **Delivery ordering** | Project `Roadmap Stage` | what must precede what | gate membership |
| **Release claim** | `threshold:*` labels | which threshold the work serves | scheduling |

**`Roadmap Stage` is delivery ordering, not threshold membership.** Stage `0 - Safety` legitimately
contains non-beta-blockers whose safety or authority work must precede later stages -- as of
2026-09-03 it held 103 items of which 82 carried `release:beta-blocker`. Reading Stage 0 as "the
beta gate" is a conflation this project has rejected explicitly, and a synchronizer that encodes
it would make the board authoritative for something it does not track.

**Threshold membership is governed separately** by the beta register and the `release:*` labels,
never inferred from a Project field.

- [ ] The synchronization contract names all five axes and their carriers, and states that none is
      derived from another.
- [ ] The synchronizer never writes one axis from another's value -- in particular it never sets
      or reads `Roadmap Stage` as a proxy for gate membership, and never re-milestones an issue to
      express a threshold.
- [ ] Divergence is reported per axis, so "readiness label disagrees with the Readiness field" is a
      distinct finding from "stage disagrees with dependency order".
- [ ] A worked negative example is recorded: a Stage 0 issue that is **not** a beta blocker is
      correct and must not be reported as drift.

## Problem

Bimaaji currently presents materially different development contracts to supported coding clients.

Measured in the Claudriel packaged-consumer installation:

- Claude receives 11 granular skills under `.claude/skills/waaseyaa-*/SKILL.md` plus generated project guidance.
- Codex receives the same detailed material flattened into a generated block in root `AGENTS.md` (about 116 KB / 3,089 generated lines).
- Codex receives no project-local `.agents/skills` inventory.
- The resulting contracts are not capability-equivalent: Claude can load focused knowledge on demand, while Codex must carry a large always-loaded context.
- The transformer design encodes client-specific output directly instead of declaring which clients support guidelines, skills, and MCP configuration.

`AGENTS.md` remains the correct Codex location for concise project-wide guidance. It is not a substitute for granular Agent Skills.

## Outcome

Waaseyaa publishes one canonical, vendor-neutral guidance and skill model, then generates capability-equivalent project-local adapters for each supported coding client.

Broad instructions remain concise and always loaded. Detailed framework knowledge is installed as on-demand skills. Unsupported capabilities are reported explicitly rather than silently flattened or omitted.

## Depends on

- [x] #2656 — canonical Bimaaji skills are package resources.

## Blocks

- #2663 — portable client/MCP descriptors require the same client capability model.
- #2664 — generated-state update and verification must understand every adapter output.
- #2665 — packaged-consumer acceptance must prove equivalent agent capability.

## Required design

Introduce an explicit adapter capability contract, conceptually:

- guidelines
- skills
- MCP configuration

Each client adapter declares the surfaces it supports and their project-local destinations. The canonical source remains vendor-neutral; generated files are compatibility outputs, not independent authorities.

Initial supported mappings:

| Client | Concise guidance | Granular skills | MCP configuration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Codex | `AGENTS.md` | `.agents/skills/waaseyaa-*/SKILL.md` | owned by #2663 |
| Claude Code | `CLAUDE.md` or marker-bounded included guidance | `.claude/skills/waaseyaa-*/SKILL.md` | owned by #2663 |

Cursor and other clients may be added only with an evidenced capability mapping; they must not inherit an assumed layout.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One canonical inventory defines every Waaseyaa skill and its source identity.
- [ ] Codex and Claude receive the same canonical skill inventory as separate, on-demand project skills.
- [ ] Root guidance contains only concise, cross-cutting instructions; detailed skill bodies are not flattened into the always-loaded file.
- [ ] Codex output uses root `AGENTS.md` plus project-local `.agents/skills`; Claude output uses its documented project guidance and `.claude/skills`.
- [ ] Client adapters declare supported capabilities instead of embedding divergent behavior in unrelated transformers.
- [ ] A client lacking a capability produces a deterministic diagnostic; Bimaaji does not silently omit or flatten that capability.
- [ ] Marker-bounded generation preserves human-authored content outside managed regions.
- [ ] Generated outputs carry source version/hash provenance and can be regenerated byte-for-byte.
- [ ] Install, update, verify, and uninstall tests cover ownership, drift, stale-file removal, and preservation of human content.
- [ ] Executable-contract tests prove every installed skill has valid metadata, references resolvable commands, and appears exactly once per supported client.
- [ ] A packaged Claudriel-style consumer test proves Codex and Claude receive equal canonical skill names and source hashes without relying on monorepo paths.
- [ ] `composer install --no-dev` leaves no Bimaaji runtime requirement or generated machine-specific configuration.
- [ ] Documentation explains the difference between always-loaded guidance, on-demand skills, and MCP tools.

## Boundaries

This issue owns guidance/skill architecture and client adapters.

It does **not**:

- implement the stdio MCP server (#2659);
- generate MCP client configuration (#2663);
- implement version-matched documentation search (#2661/#2662);
- own update orchestration or Composer hooks (#2664);
- mutate global client configuration;
- enable an HTTP MCP route;
- authorize release, deployment, or production mutation.

## Verification evidence

The closing PR must include:

1. exact candidate SHA and clean-tree status;
2. focused transformer/installer tests;
3. packaged-consumer installation for Codex and Claude;
4. inventory and source-hash equality evidence;
5. full Unit, Integration, Architecture, preflight, and changed-line coverage results;
6. explicit confirmation that human-authored project guidance survives install, update, and uninstall.

## Gap

`BodySizeLimitMiddleware` runs at priority 70, ahead of every controller and therefore ahead of `StreamableHttpTransportGuard`. For three request shapes it answers first with an oversize refusal where the guard would have refused differently — or, in one case, would not have refused at all.

Surfaced while verifying #2594. **None of these reproduces that issue's defect** — the envelope is JSON-RPC in every case, which is what #2594 was about. They are precedence differences, filed so they are recorded rather than rediscovered.

## The three cases

Verified by reading `BodySizeLimitMiddleware::process()` against `StreamableHttpTransportGuard::validate()`.

| # | Request | Answered | Guard would answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Oversize POST from a disallowed `Origin` | `413` / `REQUEST_TOO_LARGE` | `403` / `FORBIDDEN_ORIGIN` |
| 2 | `GET /mcp` with an oversize `Content-Length` | `413` / `REQUEST_TOO_LARGE` | never size-checks GET at all |
| 3 | Garbage `Content-Length` **and** a genuinely oversize body | `413` / `REQUEST_TOO_LARGE` | `400` / `-32600` Invalid Content-Length |

**#1** — the guard checks `Origin` before size, so within the guard the ordering is deliberate. The middleware precedes the guard entirely and knows nothing about origins. Arguably harmless (a rejected origin learns only that its body was too large), arguably a leak in the other direction (it confirms the endpoint exists to an origin that should have been refused flat).

**#2** — the guard's size check sits inside the POST branch, after the `GET` early return, so the transport deliberately does not size-check GET. The middleware is method-agnostic. A GET carrying a large `Content-Length` is odd, but the endpoint now answers a refusal its own transport contract does not define.

**#3** — `d3f89bdbe` added the digit-only fast-path guard precisely so a garbage header like `2000000abc` is not treated as a declared length. That works. But the backstop on the following lines (`strlen($request->getContent()) > $this->maxBytes`) then catches the body anyway, so when the header is garbage *and* the body is genuinely oversize, the answer is still the oversize code rather than the guard's Invalid Content-Length. The fast-path's stated goal is met for the header-lies-alone case and not for the both-are-wrong case.

## Severity

Cosmetic. Every case returns a well-formed JSON-RPC error in the right envelope with a plausible status; nothing is unreachable and no security boundary is weakened. A conformance harness comparing against the transport spec's own table will flag #2 and #3.

## Suggested direction

Do nothing is a legitimate outcome — say so explicitly in `docs/specs/mcp-endpoint.md` if chosen, since a reader of the guard's source would otherwise expect the guard's answer.

Otherwise the #2594 route-option seam is the natural place: a route could declare not just the refusal *vocabulary* but the precedence, or the MCP routes could opt out of the generic body check and let the guard own size for this surface — which would also resolve #2637.

## Problem

`SqliteArtifactPreparer` implements `IdentityMerge` using `INSERT OR REPLACE` against the table's primary key only. The real `user` table also has a unique `user_uuid` index. If the same stable user UUID has different numeric UIDs in the artifact and serving database, merge preparation succeeds until index restoration and then fails:

```text
UNIQUE constraint failed: user.uuid
```

This occurred with the real Sheguiandah roster: the artifact and serving rows represented the same account UUID, while the serving identity (including its password) correctly had to win.

## Required outcome

- Define stable identity keys for `IdentityMerge` (at minimum `user.uuid`) rather than assuming the primary integer key is the only identity.
- Remove/deduplicate the artifact copy of an identity before applying the destination-winning serving row.
- Preserve serving credentials and operational identity state while admitting artifact-only users.
- Reconcile or fail explicitly when UID and UUID mappings conflict with runtime account-reference tables.
- Add coverage where the same UUID has different UIDs, both tables have unique UUID indexes, and new artifact-only identities remain present.

## Impact

The documented destination-winning identity merge cannot handle the real canonical uniqueness constraints of Framework's own `user` entity.

## Problem

`SqliteArtifactPreparer` rejects valid preserved runtime state when the serving database and transport artifact have semantically compatible schemas created through different historical migration/DBAL paths. On current `main` (`d218bf6fe`), the first observed failure is:

```text
Incompatible runtime schema for _broadcast_log
```

The two `_broadcast_log` definitions differ only in SQL formatting. Further tables have SQLite-compatible affinity differences (`CLOB` versus `TEXT`) or historical constraint rendering. `schemaSignature()` hashes both raw normalized `CREATE TABLE` SQL and PRAGMA structure, so superficial SQL spelling differences remain fatal.

There is a second coupled defect: rebuilding/copying preserved tables one at a time cannot restore the configuration-authority aggregate. Its cross-table triggers reject a manifest row until the committed activation rows are present:

```text
configuration manifest evidence requires a committed activation
```

## Reproduction

Use a serving database upgraded across released Framework versions and a fresh database built from the same current Framework commit, then run `SqliteArtifactPreparer::prepare()`. Sheguiandah reproduced this with exact `d218bf6fe` code on both sides.

## Required outcome

- Distinguish semantically incompatible schema changes from harmless SQLite/DBAL rendering differences.

## Problem

A byte-for-byte SQLite snapshot copied to a different path correctly receives a different `database-identity.v1` identity. The copied configuration activation rows therefore do not bind to the clone's new `configuration.authority.v1` identity. However, the supported `waaseyaa install:init --no-interaction` recovery path cannot activate the canonical empty generation for the clone: it fails with `ConfigurationActivationConflictException: Configuration activation identity conflicted at commit` because the copied genesis activation request identity is already present under the source authority.

This leaves consumers without a supported lifecycle operation for a common disposable-clone workflow: snapshot a serving database, add synthetic verification fixtures to the copy, and boot the copy without mutating the source.

## Minimal reproduction

1. Initialize a file-backed SQLite app with `install:init`.
2. Copy the database bytes to a different real path.
3. Boot the clone using the same project root and configuration sync path.
4. Observe that active configuration is unavailable for the clone's new authority.
5. Run `install:init --no-interaction` against the clone.
6. Observe `Configuration activation identity conflicted at commit`.

## Expected

Provide a governed, auditable command or `install:init` mode that initializes/rebinds configuration authority for a cloned database identity without requiring consumers to delete `waaseyaa_config_*` lifecycle rows directly. It must not mutate the source database, silently reuse the source authority, or weaken path-bound database identity.

## Consumer evidence

Found while updating Sheguiandah Stage-1's disposable HTTP verification snapshot against Framework main `d218bf6fe41d436468f7d84fef23de2c45638f2f`. The serving artifact activates successfully; only the path-distinct verification copy is affected.

Raised from Sheg [#148](https://github.com/jonesrussell/sheguiandah-waaseyaa/issues/148) (S5 architecture program). Sheg PR: [#158](https://github.com/jonesrussell/sheguiandah-waaseyaa/pull/158).

## Gap

`Waaseyaa\Foundation\Upgrade\UpgradePreflightEvaluator` already owns the compatibility **policy**. What it does not own is turning a decision into **deterministic, comparable evidence**.

Confirmed against installed `alpha.294` and Framework `main` `9af9c7bf509962acd419dfcec3aad92c581825a4`:

- `UpgradePreflightEvaluator::evaluateBundled(array $observation): UpgradePreflightResult`
- `UpgradePreflightEvaluator::evaluate(array $contract, array $observation): UpgradePreflightResult`
- `UpgradePreflightResult` carries `decision`, `reasonCodes`, `evaluatedGates`.

There is no canonical serialization of the observation, no stable digest of it, and no versioned result envelope. Any consumer that needs to prove "the same observation produced the same decision" has to invent all three, and two consumers inventing them separately will not agree.

## Current Sheg evidence

`tools/Upgrade/S1UpgradePreflight.php` is already a thin wrapper over the framework evaluator. Sheg's `#147` map classifies it `WRAP`. Everything it adds around the evaluator is generic:

1. **Canonical observation form.** `normalize()` recursively `ksort`s every associative array while preserving list order, so key insertion order cannot change the digest.
2. **Stable digest.** `sha256:` over the canonical JSON with `JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE` plus a trailing newline.
3. **Versioned envelope.** `schema_version`, `observation_sha256`, `decision`, `reason_codes`, `evaluated_gates`.
4. **Deterministic rendering.** `canonicalJson()` for byte-identical output across runs.

The deployment recipe depends on this determinism. `deploy.php` runs `scripts/s1-upgrade-preflight.php` twice - once to decide, once again immediately before the handoff lock - and **refuses the handoff unless the observation digest and the decision are byte-identical across both runs**. That re-check is the whole point of the digest, and it is not Sheguiandah policy.

Sheg-specific and explicitly **not** part of this request: the `authorization: 'diagnostic-only'` and `staging_eligible: false` fields, which encode Sheg's own posture.

## Ownership boundary

**Framework owns** canonical observation form, the digest algorithm and its `sha256:` prefix, the versioned envelope, and deterministic rendering.

**The application owns** where the observation comes from, its own authorization posture and eligibility flags, and what it does with the decision.

## Acceptance criteria

- A public API in `Waaseyaa\Foundation\Upgrade` producing a canonical observation string and its digest, independent of key insertion order and stable across PHP versions.
- List order preserved; only associative keys sorted.
- A versioned, JSON-serializable envelope carrying at least schema version, observation digest, decision, reason codes, and evaluated gates.
- Deterministic rendering: the same observation yields byte-identical output, so a caller can compare two runs directly.
- Application-owned fields may be added to the envelope without the framework knowing them.
- Tested for: key-order independence, unicode and slash handling, list-order preservation, nested structures, and digest stability against a committed fixture.

## Non-goals

- Changing any gate, reason code, or decision semantics in `UpgradePreflightEvaluator`.
- Deciding whether an upgrade is authorized or staging-eligible - that stays with the application.
- Reading, writing, or discovering observation files.
- Any transport, CLI, or deployment orchestration.
- Signing or countersigning evidence.

## Sheg follow-up

Sheg PR #158 deliberately does **not** implement this. It moves the wrapper to `tools/Upgrade/` unchanged and keeps the `WRAP` disposition recorded. Once this seam ships on the pinned release line, Sheg reduces the wrapper to its two genuinely Sheg-specific fields.
title: foundation/upgrade: add a canonical observation digest and versioned preflight evidence envelope

body:
Raised from Sheg [#148](https://github.com/jonesrussell/sheguiandah-waaseyaa/issues/148) (S5 architecture program). Sheg PR: [#158](https://github.com/jonesrussell/sheguiandah-waaseyaa/pull/158).

## Gap

`waaseyaa/deployer` owns installing and preparing a SQLite runtime-state artifact, but nothing in the framework can **produce** a consistent standalone snapshot of a live SQLite database.

Confirmed against installed `alpha.294` and Framework `main` `9af9c7bf509962acd419dfcec3aad92c581825a4`:

- `Waaseyaa\Deployer\RuntimeState\SqliteArtifactPreparer::prepare()` - prepares an artifact that already exists.
- `Waaseyaa\Deployer\RuntimeState\SqliteArtifactInstaller` - installs one.
- `Waaseyaa\Deployer\RuntimeState\SqliteArtifactReport` - reports on one.
- `grep -r "VACUUM INTO" vendor/waaseyaa/` returns **nothing**.

So the snapshot step is missing from an otherwise complete artifact lifecycle, and every consumer must write it themselves.

## Current Sheg evidence

`tools/Stage1/SqliteArtifactSnapshot.php` (31 lines, `SqliteArtifactSnapshot::create(string $source, string $target): void`). Sheg's Stage-1 migration calls it from `scripts/stage1-migrate.php` to emit the serving-database artifact.

What it does, and why each step is load-bearing:

1. Refuses an unreadable source and refuses to overwrite an existing target.
2. `VACUUM INTO` rather than a byte copy. **A byte copy can omit committed pages that still live in the WAL.** `VACUUM INTO` asks SQLite for one transactionally consistent standalone database without modifying the source.
3. `PRAGMA quick_check` on the result, and deletes the target unless it returns `ok`.
4. Deletes a partial target if `VACUUM INTO` throws, so a failed snapshot never leaves a plausible-looking artifact behind.

Sheg's `#147` source-ownership map classifies this file `EXTRACT` / `framework-extraction-candidate`: the mechanics are entirely generic, and nothing in it is Sheguiandah policy.

## Ownership boundary

**Framework owns** the snapshot mechanism: consistency, verification, failure cleanup, and the error contract.

**The application owns** which database to snapshot, where the artifact goes, and what the artifact is subsequently used for. No application content model, migration graph, or deployment policy belongs in this seam.

## Acceptance criteria

- A public API in `waaseyaa/deployer` `RuntimeState` alongside the existing installer/preparer, taking a source path and a target path.
- Uses `VACUUM INTO`, not a file copy, so committed WAL pages are included.
- Verifies the produced snapshot before returning, and removes it if verification fails.
- Never modifies the source database, and never leaves a partial target on failure.
- Refuses an existing target rather than overwriting it.
- Distinguishes unreadable-source, target-exists, and verification-failed as separate typed failures.
- Unit tested against a real WAL-mode database with uncheckpointed committed pages, proving a byte copy would lose data and this does not.

## Non-goals

- Scheduling, retention, rotation, or pruning of snapshots.
- Encryption, compression, or transport of the artifact.
- Any Stage-1 or migration-specific behaviour.
- Changing `SqliteArtifactInstaller` or `SqliteArtifactPreparer` semantics.
- Non-SQLite drivers.

## Sheg follow-up

Sheg PR #158 deliberately does **not** implement this. It moves the class to `tools/Stage1/` unchanged and keeps the `EXTRACT` disposition recorded. Once this seam ships on the pinned release line, Sheg deletes its local copy and calls the framework API.
title: deployer: add a consistent SQLite artifact snapshot seam (VACUUM INTO) to RuntimeState

body:
## Why this audit exists

Anokii PR [#18](https://github.com/waaseyaa/anokii/pull/18) fixed a real production boot failure, but exposed a broader ownership smell:

```php
$environment = getenv('APP_ENV') ?: 'production';
$tokenSecret = AuthTokenSecret::fromRaw(getenv('AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET'));
AuthTokenSecret::assertConfiguredForEnvironment($tokenSecret, $environment);
```

The direct `getenv()` calls are consistent with Waaseyaa's current bootstrap convention: `EnvLoader` populates the process environment, `config/waaseyaa.php` reads it, and the kernel exposes the resulting configuration array. The architectural concern is that the **consumer application now owns validation and environment-classification policy that belongs beside Framework's auth implementation**. Framework's `AuthServiceProvider` independently normalizes the same secret, recognizes the same production-equivalent environments, applies fallbacks, and decides whether boot may continue.

This is likely not isolated to auth. Before adding more application-local helpers, audit the complete environment/configuration boundary across:

- `waaseyaa/framework`
- `waaseyaa/anokii`
- `jonesrussell/sheguiandah-waaseyaa` (Sheg)

This issue is broader than [#1832](https://github.com/waaseyaa/framework/issues/1832), which remains the concrete auth-token secret-custody work unit. It is also informed by Anokii [#17](https://github.com/waaseyaa/anokii/issues/17) / PR [#18](https://github.com/waaseyaa/anokii/pull/18) and the CLI/HTTP boot-parity concern recorded in [#2478](https://github.com/waaseyaa/framework/issues/2478).

## Audit scope

Pin each repository's exact `main` SHA at audit start and inventory all executable production paths involving:

1. `getenv()`, `$_ENV`, `$_SERVER`, `putenv()`, dotenv loading, and environment aliases.
2. Bootstrap configuration assembly (`config/waaseyaa.php`, entry points, `EnvLoader`, `ConfigLoader`) versus governed runtime configuration (`ConfigFactory`, `EnvironmentConfigFactory`, sync/active configuration).
3. Direct environment reads after kernel configuration has already been assembled.
4. Application-local parsing, normalization, validation, defaults, and fail-open/fail-closed policy that duplicate or contradict Framework package policy.
5. Secret acquisition, fallback, derivation, custody, redaction, serialization, logging, and placeholder rejection.
6. Environment classification (`production`, `staging`, `local`, `dev`, `development`, `testing`, unknown values) and duplicated classification lists.
7. Omitted key versus `null`, `false`, empty string, whitespace, malformed value, and placeholder behavior.
8. CLI, HTTP, worker, queue, test, and generated/packaged application parity.
9. Naming drift and aliases such as `environment`, `app_env`, `APP_ENV`, `AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET`, `WAASEYAA_*`, and consumer-specific equivalents.
10. Tests or fixtures that bypass the production resolution path and therefore cannot detect policy drift.

Classify every confirmed site as one of:

- legitimate bootstrap adapter;
- Framework-owned policy;
- application-owned composition;
- duplicated/drifted policy;
- post-bootstrap environment bypass;
- test-only override;
- unresolved/needs design.

Do not infer safety from naming or comments. Trace each value from source to consumer and verify precedence and failure behavior.

## Required evidence

- A committed, reproducible audit report pinned to all three repository SHAs.
- A machine-readable or mechanically checkable inventory of confirmed executable sites, with repository, file, line, variable/config key, phase, consumer, policy owner, classification, and disposition.
- Counts derived from the committed inventory rather than hand-maintained prose.
- A resolution matrix covering process-injected variables, `.env`, missing values, empty values, malformed values, and unknown environments.
- At least one real CLI boot and one real HTTP/worker boot parity rehearsal per application for security- or boot-critical configuration.
- Explicit examination of secret leakage through exceptions, logs, debug output, config dumps, cache artifacts, test output, and serialization.
- Verification of whether `EnvironmentConfigFactory` is being mistaken for the bootstrap-secret boundary anywhere; document the intended boundary clearly.
- A comparison against the established `ApplicationSecret` custody pattern and a decision on which secrets require purpose-derived keys versus independent operator-owned secrets.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Framework, Anokii, and Sheg are audited at pinned SHAs; no repository is represented only by search counts.
- [ ] Every production `getenv()` / `$_ENV` / `$_SERVER` read in scope has an evidence-backed owner and disposition.
- [ ] Duplicated environment classification and secret-validation rules are identified, including the Anokii `AuthTokenSecret` seed case.
- [ ] Bootstrap configuration and governed content/configuration are clearly separated; no recommendation moves bootstrap secrets into syncable configuration.
- [ ] The canonical precedence and normalization contract is specified for each security- or boot-critical value.
- [ ] CLI, HTTP, worker, and test paths are shown to use the same resolved policy or have an explicitly justified difference.
- [ ] Each confirmed defect or design decision becomes a bounded issue in the owning repository, linked back here, with dependency order and migration compatibility stated.
- [ ] A regression-prevention proposal is included (architecture test, static checker, typed boundary, or a justified combination), without weakening legitimate application composition.
- [ ] The report distinguishes findings requiring code changes from documentation-only ambiguity and accepted risk.
- [ ] The audit is independently reviewed before this issue is closed.

## Expected architectural outcome

Applications should remain responsible for declaring deployment values and application-specific composition. Framework packages should own normalization, validation, environment sensitivity, security semantics, and typed access for the policies they implement. Environment reads should be concentrated at an explicit bootstrap boundary; runtime consumers should receive resolved configuration or typed secret/configuration objects rather than independently re-reading process state.

## Summary

Two CFG-02 authorization seams still have no production producer and keep their refusing defaults:

- `ConfigurationRollbackValidatorInterface` → `RefusingConfigurationRollbackValidator`
- `ConfigurationCandidateSweepAuthorizerInterface` → `RefusingConfigurationCandidateSweepAuthorizer`

So `DatabaseConfigurationActivator` can activate an ordinary verified bundle (#2430) but cannot reactivate a retained generation, and cannot sweep staged candidates.

## Why they were left out of #2430

#2430 restored the *forward* path: a protected signer authorizes the bytes, explicit CLI execution authorizes the timing, and the result is a new generation that removes nothing. Neither of these fits that shape.

**Rollback** reactivates content that was already superseded. The original signature is immutable provenance, but it says nothing about whether returning to that content *now* is safe — the schema cohort may have moved, and readable-versus-writable contract versions differ deliberately. The activator already refuses to let a rollback carry a fresh bundle (`Retained-generation rollback must not replace immutable signature provenance`), so a rollback policy has to authorize a *transition*, not a payload.

**Candidate sweep** deletes staged rows. It is maintenance over activation bookkeeping rather than over configuration content, so signature-based reasoning does not apply to it at all.

## What each policy has to decide

Rollback:
- Who may authorize returning to a retained generation, and against what expected active token.
- Whether the target generation's package-contract cohort must still be readable by the installed cohort.
- Whether rollback is bounded (last N generations, or a retention window).

Candidate sweep:
- Which lifecycle states are sweepable (`staged`, `superseded`) and after how long.
- Whether sweep may run unattended (scheduler) or requires an operator.

## Related

- #2430 restored the ordinary verified activation path.
- #2432 covers destructive import, which is a third distinct policy.

## Summary

`VerifiedNonDestructiveConfigurationActivationAuthorizer` (#2430) authorizes ordinary activation of a verified signed bundle that deletes nothing. An import carrying tombstones — which is how `config:import --delete-orphans` expresses removal — is refused:

```
Configuration activation that deletes N active entries is not authorized.
A signature proves what the new content is, never that removing existing content is intended.
Destructive import policy is a separate decision.
```

## Why it was left out of #2430

A signature over a bundle proves what the new content *is*. It does not prove that an active entry absent from that bundle was meant to be removed rather than simply not authored in this pass. Folding deletion into the same authority would have made "signed" silently mean "signed, and also authorized to delete anything not mentioned", which is a materially different and much larger claim.

## What a policy has to decide

- Whether deletion needs a distinct signal from the operator beyond `--delete-orphans` (a second, explicitly destructive signed artifact? an expected-deletion manifest the signer authorized?).
- Whether the signer or the operator authorizes *which* entries may go, given the activator already requires a content-bound tombstone per omitted entry.
- Whether deletion is permitted at all outside a maintenance window or a distinct role.

## Current behaviour

Non-destructive import works end to end (`tests/PackagedForm/check-verified-config-import`). Destructive import refuses with the message above. No data is at risk; the gap is that a consumer cannot remove configuration through the governed path.

## Problem  Waaseyaa already has a strong repository-native specification system: enduring contracts in `docs/specs/`, GitHub anchor issues, design-first development, TDD, `spec-reviewed:` commit trailers, drift detection, and CI enforcement. However, specification structure varies by subsystem, and acceptance requirements are not always expressed in a form that maps cleanly to executable evidence.  Adding OpenSpec, GitHub Spec Kit, BMAD, Agent OS, or another workflow runtime now would create overlapping sources of truth and new generated-agent/update machinery shortly after Spec Kitty was retired. The useful ideas from those systems can be adopted without adopting their runtimes.  ## Decision  Strengthen Waaseyaa's native specification contract incrementally. Keep `docs/specs/` authoritative, GitHub as the execution and audit surface, and existing repository gates as enforcement. Do not introduce a new specification framework as part of this work.  ## Goals  - Establish a concise canonical template for new or materially changed `docs/specs/` contracts. - Make requirements, invariants, failure behavior, and verification evidence easy for humans and coding agents to identify. - Improve traceability from anchor issue to specification requirement to test or operational evidence. - Apply the contract incrementally when specifications are touched; avoid a bulk rewrite of the existing corpus. - Preserve the current design-first workflow and source-to-spec drift detector.  ## Proposed specification shape  The canonical template should cover, where applicable:  1. Purpose 2. Scope and non-goals 3. Normative requirements 4. Invariants 5. Failure behavior 6. Security and authorization boundaries 7. Compatibility, migration, and rollback 8. Acceptance scenarios 9. Verification mapping  Normative language should have stable meaning:  - `MUST`: enforced contract - `SHOULD`: default with a documented exception path - `MAY`: optional behavior  Behavioral scenarios should use a lightweight GIVEN / WHEN / THEN form. This is a Markdown convention, not a dependency on Gherkin or a test generator.  Example:  ```markdown ### Requirement: Unknown hooks are preserved  The installer MUST refuse to overwrite an unrecognized Git hook.  #### Scenario: A custom pre-push hook exists  - GIVEN an unmarked pre-push hook - WHEN the operator runs the installer - THEN installation fails - AND the existing hook remains byte-identical ```  ## Change and PR traceability  For substantial work, the PR should map each normative requirement to a test or other evidence, for example:  | Requirement | Test or evidence | |---|---| | Unknown hooks are preserved | `ProjectHooksTest::installer_is_idempotent_and_preserves_unknown_hooks` | | Startup context is bounded | `ProjectHooksTest::claude_context_is_bounded_and_works_from_a_subdirectory` |  This mapping may live in the PR body or a verification artifact; it should not create a second enduring specification tree.  ## Non-goals  - Do not install or initialize OpenSpec, Spec Kit, BMAD, Agent OS, or Spec Kitty. - Do not move or duplicate `docs/specs/` into another tool-owned directory. - Do not bulk-convert all existing specifications. - Do not require every typo, dependency bump, or mechanical refactor to produce a specification. - Do not generate implementation code from specifications.  ## Implementation outline  1. Add a repository-native specification template and document when each section is required. 2. Update `docs/specs/workflow.md` and `CLAUDE.md` with the incremental adoption rule. 3. Extend the PR template with an optional requirement-to-evidence table for substantive changes. 4. Add a lightweight changed-spec validator or architecture test that checks only new or materially changed specifications and fails with actionable messages. 5. Pilot the template on one real bounded framework change. 6. Review the pilot for agent comprehension, reviewer usefulness, document churn, and false-positive gate behavior before expanding enforcement.  ## Acceptance criteria  - [ ] `docs/specs/` remains the only authoritative enduring specification tree. - [ ] A canonical Waaseyaa specification template is committed and documented. - [ ] New or materially changed specifications have identifiable normative requirements and verification mappings where applicable. - [ ] A lightweight validator covers changed specifications without forcing a bulk rewrite. - [ ] The validator has self-tests proving both a valid example and each enforced failure class. - [ ] The PR template supports requirement-to-evidence traceability without burdening trivial changes. - [ ] One bounded pilot demonstrates the complete issue -> spec -> implementation -> evidence -> PR path. - [ ] Existing specifications remain valid until materially touched. - [ ] No new specification-framework runtime or generated agent-command tree is added. - [ ] Active workflow documentation and changelog are updated, and the full verification suite passes.  ## Future reconsideration trigger  Re-evaluate a dedicated specification tool only if cross-repository planning becomes a repeated operational problem that the native GitHub plus `docs/specs/` workflow cannot solve cleanly. **Non-blocking.** Row and field access remain correctly denied; this is about *schema* visibility only. Filed for a deliberate decision rather than as a defect to fix under time pressure.

Found on `v0.1.0-alpha.283` while verifying that a downstream app's private entity types stay closed on every generic read surface.

## What is and is not exposed

The app (RHT Circle's Sagamok monitor) registers seven entity types whose access policy grants only a bespoke ability and **never** `view`. Verified against a database holding 4 items and 1 issue that the app's own dashboard renders:

```
{monitorItemList{items{id title}total}}   ->  {"items": [], "total": 0}
{monitorItem(id: 1){id title}}            ->  {"monitorItem": null}
{monitorIssueList{items{title severity}}} ->  {"items": []}
```

**Data access is closed.** No row, and no field — including `Internal` fields such as `severity` — is reachable. JSON:API, `/api/discovery/*` and the SSR entity catch-all all return 404 for the same types.

## What is visible

GraphQL's schema still carries the types, and error hints name them:

```
{monitorItems{id}}
-> Cannot query field "monitorItems" on type "Query".
   Did you mean "monitorItem", "monitorItemList", "monitorEvent", or "monitorIssue"?
```

So an anonymous caller can learn that entity types called `monitor_item`, `monitor_event` and `monitor_issue` exist, and can enumerate their field names through introspection, without obtaining a single row.

## Why it may be worth a decision

For most applications this is uninteresting — schema shape is not secret. It is worth an explicit choice because:

- an entity type's **name** can itself carry meaning. `monitor_issue` and `portal_access_state` describe what an organisation is being asked about, which is information even with zero rows attached;
- the framework already treats `discoverable: false` and the entity-type disable mechanism as *not* protection (documented, and correctly so). This is the same category: a reader could reasonably assume a type nobody can read is also a type nobody can see, and that assumption is currently wrong;
- it interacts with `FieldReadLevel`. A field declared `Internal` is unreadable, yet its **name** appears in the schema, which is a small asymmetry worth stating one way or the other.

## Options

1. **Document it explicitly** — state in the access-control and GraphQL specs that schema shape is public for every registered type regardless of policy, so applications with sensitive type names know to plan for it. Cheapest, and may well be the right answer.
2. **Filter the schema by policy** — omit types no anonymous caller can read from the anonymous schema. Correct-feeling but expensive: schema construction would become account-dependent, which affects caching and introspection tooling.
3. **Opt-out flag** — let a type declare itself schema-private, in the same spirit as `api: false`. Narrow, and matches how the framework already lets a type decline JSON:API.

I would suggest **1** unless someone has a concrete case for the others; the downstream app is not blocked either way.

## Not a workaround request

RHT Circle needs nothing here. Its data boundary holds, is asserted route-by-route in `NoAutoExposureTest`, and the empty results above were produced against a populated database. This issue exists so the framework's position on schema visibility is recorded rather than incidental.

## Environment

- `waaseyaa/framework` `v0.1.0-alpha.283`
- Verified over real HTTP against a booted kernel, anonymous caller, no dev-fallback account

body:
## Summary

On v0.1.0-alpha.276, a content-group entity type declared with the attribute API (`#[ContentEntityType(api: true)]`, registered `group: 'content'`) whose `status` field uses the scaffold default (`read: FieldReadLevel::Public`, no `authorizationInput` setting) is invisible to anonymous JSON:API reads even when published: `GET /api/{type}` returns 200 with `data: []` and `GET /api/{type}/{id}` returns the concealed 404. The documented recipe "group: 'content' + status = 1 + api: true => anonymous read" does not hold for these types.

## Production-shaped reproduction

Observed on waaseyaa.org's CI container (php:8.5-cli-alpine, APP_ENV=production, real boot gates), framework v0.1.0-alpha.276:

1. Entity type `release` with `#[ContentEntityType(id: 'release', api: true)]`, registered via `EntityType::fromClass(Release::class, revisionable: true, revisionDefault: true, group: 'content')`; `status` field declared `#[Field(label: 'Published', read: FieldReadLevel::Public)] public bool $status = true;`.
2. Create + save a published row (repository layer).
3. `curl http://.../api/release` as anonymous.

Result: HTTP 200, `"data": [], "meta": {"total": 0}`. The same rows render fine on HTML pages and via app-level MCP tools that read through the repository directly.

## Root cause

- `EntityAccessHandler::check()` routes every `view` decision for an `AuthorizationPrincipal` through the protected-entity-read path whenever any applicable policy implements `ProtectedReadPolicyProviderInterface` (access/src/EntityAccessHandler.php, `check()` first branch). `PublishedContentAccessPolicy::protectedEntityReadPolicy()` is never null, so this path is always taken for content-group types, and the ordinary policy loop (where `PublishedContentAccessPolicy::access()` would return Allowed for published rows) is unreachable.
- The compiled policy subject only carries a field when that field declares `settings: ['authorizationInput' => true]` (entity/src/EntityReadRuntime.php), which the framework requires to be paired with `read: FieldReadLevel::Protected`.
- Framework-shipped `Node` follows exactly that pattern (`status` is Protected + authorizationInput, node/src/Node.php:63), which is why nodes work. But `MakeContentTypeHandler` (cli/src/Handler/MakeContentTypeHandler.php) scaffolds `status` without `authorizationInput`, and nothing warns at registration time, so every scaffolded or attribute-authored content type silently ships an anonymous-empty API.
- With `status` absent from the subject, the protected read resolves Neutral ("No protected entity-read policy provided an opinion") which downstream treats as denied: `JsonApiController::index()` filters the row, `show()` conceals with 404.

## Impact

Any consuming app that follows the attribute tutorial or `make:content-type` and sets `api: true` gets a live, allowlist-validated JSON:API surface that returns no data to anonymous callers, with no error anywhere. waaseyaa.org hit this with three types (`release`, `roadmap_item`, `case_study`) and is withdrawing `api: true` until this is resolved.

## Possible directions (not prescriptive)

- Have the protected-entity-read path fall back to the ordinary policy loop when the subject carries none of the declared inputs, instead of resolving Neutral.
- Or make `PublishedContentStatusReader` readable in that path from raw values as it already is in `PublishedContentAccessPolicy::access()`.
- Or make `make:content-type` scaffold `status` as Protected + authorizationInput like `Node`, and fail registration loudly when a content-group `api: true` type's status field will never reach the read subject.

Reported from waaseyaa/waaseyaa-org PR #13, where the reproduction and container evidence live.

---

## Acceptance criteria (added 2026-09-03, from release-train planning)

This issue is Lane 4 work package **A10b** — its own reviewed repair, sequenced before the packaged Studio-alpha harness (#2789) and deliberately **not** folded into the `make:content-type` migration, because an access-control change of unknown shape inside the generation-engine migration would make that PR unreviewably heterogeneous.

### Why the shape is unknown

The scaffolded `Published` field lacks `authorizationInput` and `FieldReadLevel::Protected` (`MakeContentTypeHandler.php:189`, versus `Node.php:63`). But `EntityAccessHandler` takes the protected-entity-read branch for **every** VIEW whenever any applicable policy implements `ProtectedReadPolicyProviderInterface`, which makes the ordinary policy loop unreachable. Whether the correct repair is two lines in the scaffold template or a change to policy composition is **not yet known**, and settling that is the first deliverable.

### Approach — the failing test comes first

Open with a focused failing integration test: create a generated content type, publish an entity of it, read it as an anonymous client through the real HTTP route with `WAASEYAA_DEV_FALLBACK_ACCOUNT` unset, and assert rows are returned. That test settles template-edit-versus-redesign before any fix is authored, and becomes the regression guard afterwards.

### Criteria

- [ ] A failing integration test exists that asserts an anonymous read of a published, generated content type returns rows through a real route.
- [ ] The test passes, and the PR body states which of the two shapes the repair turned out to be.
- [ ] A generated type's published-read behaviour matches `Node`'s for the same field configuration — asserted by test, not by inspection.
- [ ] **Required negative test:** an unpublished entity of a generated type is **not** readable anonymously. Fixing the published read must not open an unpublished one — a read-path repair is precisely where that regression hides.
- [ ] If the repair touches `EntityAccessHandler` or policy composition, its blast radius is stated in the PR body, and the existing protected-read behaviour for `Node` is covered by a test that would fail if it regressed.
- [ ] `php bin/check-pr-preflight` exits 0; the Unit, Integration and Architecture suites pass on the exact pushed head.

### Acceptance evidence must not run with a dev fallback

Any acceptance run with `WAASEYAA_DEV_FALLBACK_ACCOUNT` set is invalid for this issue — the fallback masks exactly the field-read denial under test.

body:
Four findings from hardening a consumer app's body render paths. They are filed together because they are the same underlying shape: the framework owns a good sanitizer, but the surfaces around it let a consumer end up outside its protection without noticing. Environment: framework `0.1.0-alpha.274`, PHP 8.5.8, consumer is a migrated WordPress site with custom render pipelines. --- ## (a) `EntityRenderer` exposes an unsanitized `fields.*.raw` beside `fields.*.formatted` `vendor/waaseyaa/ssr/src/EntityRenderer.php:148` puts both into the Twig context. `formatted` goes through `HtmlFormatter`, which sanitizes properly: ```php // vendor/waaseyaa/ssr/src/Formatter/HtmlFormatter.php:25 return $this->sanitizer->sanitize($html); ``` Verified on payloads: `` becomes `''`, `` becomes ``, `x` becomes `x`. `raw` gets none of that. Any template doing `{{ fields.body.raw|raw }}` emits stored HTML verbatim. Nothing in the name warns about it, and it sits directly beside the safe one, so it reads like "the original value" rather than "the unsanitized value". **Ask:** drop `raw`, or rename it so the danger is in the name (`unsanitized`), or restrict it to non-HTML field types. --- ## (b) The sanitizer is not available as an injectable service with a composable config There are two sanitizer configs in the framework and no way for a consumer to extend either: - `Waaseyaa\SSR\Formatter\HtmlFormatter` builds its own in the constructor. - `Waaseyaa\Api\Sanitizer\RichTextSanitizer` builds its own: `allowSafeElements()->forceHttpsUrls()`. Both are private to their class. A consumer whose controllers render bodies themselves (custom pipeline, migration-specific normalization) cannot reuse either, so it must construct a third `HtmlSanitizerConfig`. That is exactly what we had to do, and the result is a second allowlist for one field type that can silently diverge from the framework's. Concretely, our config has to differ from `RichTextSanitizer`'s in ways that are legitimate for migrated content: `class`/`id` (page-builder markup styles by class, and view models XPath `.sfn-card` out of stored bodies), relative URLs (migrated links are localized to root-relative), inline SVG (page-builder icons, and one published post carries 662 characters of visible prose in SVG `` children), and the WAI-ARIA attribute set. Those are deviations we want to be reviewable as a delta. Today they can only be expressed as a rebuild. **Ask:** expose the sanitizer as an injectable service, and expose the baseline config as something a consumer can extend, so a custom render pipeline can start from the framework's allowlist rather than reinventing it. --- ## (c) Admin-surface sanitization keys on field type; the SPA's innerHTML keys on widget; nothing enforces agreement This is the one with a live exploit path. Sanitization gate (`vendor/waaseyaa/api/src/ResourceSerializer.php:284`): ```php if ($type !== null && RichTextSanitizer::isHtmlFieldType($type)) { $attributes[$name] = $this->richTextSanitizer->sanitizeValue($value); ``` with `RichTextSanitizer::HTML_FIELD_TYPES = ['text_long']`. Client sink (`vendor/waaseyaa/admin-surface/dist/_nuxt/CTR2qBz0.js`, `SchemaView`): ```js c["x-widget"]==="richtext" && e(l)[a] ? (n(),o("dd",{ class:"field-value field-value--html", innerHTML:e(l)[a] },...)) ``` So the server sanitizes on **field type** and the client injects HTML on **widget**. They agree today only by convention. Declaring `'x-widget' => 'richtext'` on a field whose type is not `text_long` yields stored XSS in an administrator's browser with no other change. Proof that the gate is currently the only barrier: with payloads stored raw in a node body (byte-identical, 308 bytes), `GET /admin/_surface/node/{uuid}` returns ```

BEGIN

\n\n\n\nx\n\n

END

``` for both a scoped operator and an administrator. Remove or narrow that one call and the SPA innerHTMLs the stored payload. **Ask:** derive the widget from the field type (or refuse to emit a `richtext` widget for a type the sanitizer does not gate), and/or sanitize on the widget contract rather than the type. Client-side sanitization at the sink would be defence in depth, not a substitute. --- ## (d) `SecurityHeadersMiddleware` supports CSP but the kernel hardcodes it off, with no config seam `vendor/waaseyaa/foundation/src/Middleware/SecurityHeadersMiddleware.php:23` has a working CSP parameter, defaulted sensibly: ```php public function __construct( private readonly ?string $csp = "default-src 'self'", ``` But `vendor/waaseyaa/foundation/src/Kernel/HttpKernel.php:506` constructs it as: ```php new SecurityHeadersMiddleware( csp: null, hstsEnabled: false, frameOptions: is_array($this->config['security_headers'] ?? null) && is_string($this->config['security_headers']['frame_options'] ?? null) ? $this->config['security_headers']['frame_options'] : 'SAMEORIGIN', ), ``` `frame_options` is read from app config; `csp` is hardcoded `null`. So no response carries a Content-Security-Policy and a consumer has no supported way to turn one on. We wanted CSP as a `frame-src` backstop behind an iframe allowlist decision and could not enable it without forking the kernel or bolting on a second middleware, so we left it off and are reporting it instead. **Ask:** read `csp` from `config['security_headers']` the same way `frame_options` already is. --- Happy to supply the consumer-side reproduction scripts for (c) if useful.

## Current backlog disposition (2026-08-16)

**Measurable outcome:** Define one consumer asset-manifest schema and helper contract for URL resolution, preload metadata, versioning, and missing-asset failure.

**Dependencies / links:** Feeds starter/frontend work such as #1626 and must align with existing Admin distribution ownership.

**Why this is not ready:** Manifest ownership, supported build tools, and compatibility behavior are not specified.

**Authority boundary:** This disposition preserves the idea; it does not authorize implementation, release, deployment, production activation, or operational mutation.

---

## Original report (preserved)

## Summary

Consumers serving hashed/fingerprinted public assets (CSS/JS) have **no framework-provided way to resolve a logical asset name to its current content-hashed URL**, and no shared guidance on cache headers for those assets. This surfaced as the **SFN stale-CSS-after-deploy incident (2026-07-24)**: after a deploy, browsers kept serving the previous CSS because the asset URL was stable while its bytes changed, and nothing invalidated it.

SFN worked around this with a consumer-side `PublicAssetVersioner`. That seam is the **interim reference** the framework should absorb into a first-class helper so every consumer doesn't reinvent it.

## Proposed helper

- **Content-hash manifest**: a build/generate step that emits a manifest mapping logical asset paths → content-hashed output paths (e.g. `app.css` → `app.4f3a91c2.css`). Manifest format TBD (JSON keyed by logical path).
- **Template `asset()` helper**: a Twig (and/or SSR) function that resolves a logical name to the hashed URL via the manifest, so templates reference `asset('app.css')` and always emit the current fingerprinted URL. Graceful fallback to the un-hashed path when no manifest entry exists (dev).
- **Cache-header guidance**: documented convention — long-lived immutable caching (`Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`) for content-hashed assets, since the hash *is* the cache-buster; and short/no-cache for the HTML that references them. Pair with the existing `ETagMiddleware` story.

## Scope

Backlog / design-first — **no implementation in this issue**. Needs a `docs/specs/` entry (work-surface / infrastructure asset story) and a decision on where the manifest generation lives (build tooling vs. runtime). Absorb SFN's `PublicAssetVersioner` as the interim consumer-side seam / prior art.

## Motivating incident

SFN stale-CSS-after-deploy, 2026-07-24 — stable asset URLs served cached CSS after a deploy; no framework manifest/`asset()` helper to fingerprint-bust it.

## Motivation

Chat is becoming table-stakes for applications, and every Waaseyaa app currently hand-rolls it. Minoo ships a working, production-deployed **cite-only corpus chat** (minoo #822) built entirely from framework primitives plus app glue — evidence that the framework is one composed feature away from offering this first-class. Product direction from Russell (2026-07-16): chat is integral to Minoo going forward and "should be a first-class Waaseyaa feature."

## What already exists in the framework

- `waaseyaa/messaging` — threads, participants (unique-constrained since alpha.263), creator-seeding (alpha.255)
- SSE broadcasting — `BroadcastStorage` / `BroadcastRouter` (auth-gated since alpha.250)
- `waaseyaa/ai-agent` — agent runs with tool allowlists (alpha.261) for assistant-style chats
- Access layer — entity/field gates, fail-closed query account binding

What's missing is the **composed feature**: a conversation surface + server contract + a grounding seam.

## Prior art in Minoo (offered as the reference consumer)

- `App\Http\Controller\Chat\ChatController` — cite-only chat over the dictionary corpus: responses are retrieval-grounded and citation-bearing, never free generation
- **Consent-gated retrieval at the entity layer** — anonymous callers only ever see published, public-consent rows; the OCAP boundary lives in the access policy, not the controller
- The **#788 lesson** (minoo): `loadMultiple([])` fail-open semantics caused a real consent leak into a chat surface; the regression pattern (fail-closed empty-set handling) is exactly what a framework seam must make the default

## Proposed shape (for design discussion, not implementation)

A `waaseyaa/chat` package composing messaging (persistence) + broadcasting (delivery) + access (gating):

1. Conversation API routes + SSR/admin surfaces
2. A **retrieval-grounding interface** apps implement to plug corpus/RAG sources — fail-closed by contract: the seam receives the request account and every grounding read is access-checked; empty result sets stay empty
3. Optional `ai-agent` integration behind the same allowlist discipline
4. Cite-only mode as a first-class configuration (grounded responses carry source citations; no citation → no claim)

## Asks

- Design-first discussion on package boundary (L3 vs L4) and the grounding-seam contract
- Minoo volunteers as first consumer and will contribute its consent-gating patterns
- No implementation until the design is accepted

**Measurable outcome:** Split and define the media source-plugin interface separately from the authorized-download transport, each with capability and lifecycle acceptance.

**Dependencies / links:** Depends on the #1742 CAS/durability decision and current media access contracts.

---

## Original report (preserved)

**Type:** net-new FEATURE (not remediation/cleanup). Tracked out of the audit-remediation campaign per the claim-vs-code correction below.

## Background

`MediaType` declares a `source` plugin id (`'file'`/`'image'`/`'oembed'`) + `sourceConfiguration`, and its docblock advertised that "each media type is associated with a media source plugin that handles the specific media handling logic." **That system is not implemented:** there is no `MediaSourceInterface`, no plugin, no registry, no resolver that maps a media entity → file URI, and no media-create flow in the framework (the upload endpoint produces a decoupled `File` sidecar; consuming apps create media entities themselves).

The docs have been corrected to stop advertising source-plugin resolution / gated media downloads as working (claim-vs-code fix). This issue tracks building the real feature.

## Scope

1. **Media source-plugin substrate:** a `MediaSourceInterface` + concrete `file`/`image` (and later `oembed`) source plugins + a registry, resolving a media entity (by its `MediaType.source` + `sourceConfiguration`) to its file URI — the single source of truth for media file location (no duplicate `source_uri` field).
2. **Authorized media download:** `GET /media/{id}/download`, mirroring the attachment slice shipped in #1761 — **reuse `Waaseyaa\Attachment\Storage\PrivateFileStore`** + the same deny-by-default / fail-closed / 404-on-deny pattern + the `private://` scheme, resolving the file URI via the source plugin from (1). Add a `private://` opt-in to media uploads.
3. Public assets (e.g. avatars) stay `public://` + the host's static path, unaffected.

## Why it's a feature, not a cleanup blocker

The sensitive-file security gap that motivated CL-13 is already closed for **attachment** (#1761). Media files currently serve from `public://` with no authorized-download path — a feature gap, not a reachable defect (no doc now claims otherwise). Building a whole plugin system is net-new product work outside the remediation campaign.

## References

- Attachment precedent + reusable `PrivateFileStore`: #1761
- CL-13 design: `docs/audits/cl13-private-file-bytes-design.md`

**Tracked from WP18 (framework-cleanup-alpha245). Deferred functional gap, NOT fixed in WP18 (docs only). No beta timing is implied.**

## Summary

The media versioning/CAS pipeline is wired structurally but its input trigger is never called, and its pending store is non-durable.

## Evidence ( grounded in code )

- `MediaServiceProvider` registers the `MediaVersionType` entity type, wires `MediaCascadeDeleteSubscriber`, and binds `ContentAddressedFileRepositoryDecorator` — so the *machinery* exists and is wired.
- A media version is created on save by reading `$this->pendingUploads[$mediaUuid]` (`MediaVersionStorageDriver.php:88` → `createVersion()` → `cas->write()`).
- **The only way bytes enter that pipeline is `MediaVersionStorageDriver::setPendingUpload()` (line 65) — and it has ZERO production callers** (no controller / `UploadHandler` / route calls it; only the class's own doc + tests reference it). So versioning never fires on a real upload.
- **`private array $pendingUploads = []` (line 42) is a per-request in-memory map.** Even if a caller set a pending upload, it would not survive across requests — a latent data-loss risk if wired naively.

## Deferred functional work

1. Invoke `setPendingUpload()` from the live upload path (`UploadHandler` / the media upload controller) so an uploaded blob actually enters CAS versioning.
2. Replace the per-request in-memory `$pendingUploads` with a durable hand-off (or restructure so bytes are written to CAS synchronously during upload).

## Scope note

Per WP18 scoping the media README is left unchanged — it makes **no** versioning claim, so there is no doc over-claim to retract. This issue captures the underlying functional gap only.

Refs: `packages/media/src/Version/MediaVersionStorageDriver.php:42,65,88,103`.

- compares the presented token with a plain array key lookup (`$this->tokens[$token] ?? null`) — not a constant-time compare;

## Current backlog disposition (2026-08-16)

**Measurable outcome:** Define an application-owned server-rendered head contribution hook with deterministic precedence, escaping, and cache behavior.

**Dependencies / links:** Cross-linked with #2342: the Open Graph package cannot own app integration until this hook boundary is decided.

**Why this is not ready:** Renderer ownership and middleware/controller timing remain unresolved.

**Authority boundary:** This disposition preserves the idea; it does not authorize implementation, release, deployment, production activation, or operational mutation.

---

## Original report (preserved)

**Context.** Building an Inertia app (Wiisnin) we needed server-rendered OpenGraph/Twitter `<head>` meta so pasted links unfurl on Facebook etc. (scrapers never run the Vue `<Head>`). The `seo` package builds the meta fine, but there is **no clean app seam to put it in the SERVED `<head>`**. Two dead ends:

**1. Provider middleware runs in the authorization pipeline, BEFORE controller dispatch.** `HttpKernel` collects `HasMiddlewareInterface` middleware (including from app providers) and runs the pipeline against a dummy inner handler that returns an empty 200 (`HttpKernel.php` ~L341–366):
```php
$pipeline->handle($httpRequest, new class implements HttpHandlerInterface {
    public function handle(HttpRequest $r): HttpResponse { return new HttpResponse('', 200); }
});
```
The real controller/Inertia HTML is produced *after* this pipeline (the dispatcher, ~L427). So app middleware can authorize / short-circuit but can **never post-process the rendered HTML** — it never sees `</head>`.

**2. An app provider can't override the Inertia full-page renderer.** `resolveInertiaFullPageRenderer()` returns the **first** provider that binds `InertiaFullPageRendererInterface`, and root/app providers from `extra.waaseyaa.providers` are appended **after** package providers (`PackageManifestCompiler` ~L621). So the package `InertiaServiceProvider` renderer always wins; binding our own is ignored.

Net: no post-dispatch response filter, and no per-request "head contributions" the controller can populate, for app-rendered `<head>` content.

**Workaround (Wiisnin).** Inject in the front controller `public/index.php` — the one post-dispatch hook the app owns — after `$kernel->handle()`:
```php
try { \App\Http\SeoInjector::inject($response, $projectRoot); } catch (\Throwable) {}
```
`SeoInjector` checks GET + text/html + has `</head>`, derives the route's vendor via a **read-only SQLite/PDO** lookup (it has no kernel services from index.php), builds og/twitter via the `seo` `MetaTagBuilder` + manual tags, and rewrites `</head>`. Verified by curl — but it's a hack (raw PDO in the front controller, duplicated routing knowledge).

**Suggested fix (any one):**
- A **post-dispatch response filter** hook for providers (middleware that wraps the real controller response, not the auth dummy), or
- A **head-contributions bag** the controller populates (e.g. `Inertia::share`-style head, or a response attribute) that the Inertia root template renders server-side, or
- Let app providers override `InertiaFullPageRendererInterface` (resolve app bindings first / a dedicated head-renderer hook).

Related: #1626 (Inertia on-ramp), #1623 (app-vs-package provider resolution order).

*Field report from building Wiisnin (Inertia+Vue) on alpha.192. Raw: WAASEYAA-FRICTION.md F-26.*

## Original report (preserved)

Three entity-modeling decisions a new app hits with no guidance. Grouping as one docs issue.

**1. `relationship` package vs a foreign-key field.** The `relationship` package models a relationship as its own entity record (`from_entity_type/id` → `to_entity_type/id`) — a knowledge-graph edge, not a foreign key. For simple belongs-to ownership (menu item → vendor, order line → order) that means an extra record + lookup per association and no natural cascade. We used plain integer FK fields instead (queried via `json_extract`; see #1610 / `FieldStorage::Data`). Document when to reach for `relationship` vs an FK field, and consider a documented belongs-to helper.

**2. Reserved-word entity-type ids.** Registering an entity type `order` creates a table named `order`, a SQL reserved word. Save/find round-trip fine because the storage layer quotes identifiers (verified), but it's a latent footgun for any hand-written SQL or migration that doesn't quote. Note reserved-word handling in the entity-type docs (or emit a warning for reserved-word ids).

**3. Per-entity-scoped taxonomy.** The spec for our app wanted "a `menu_category` vocabulary scoped per vendor." `Term` has a fixed field set, so you can't add a `vendor_id` to a term without extending the framework entity. The pragmatic answer is a shared vocabulary with app-layer scoping (or per-owner vocabularies, which explodes ids). Document the shared-vocab + app-scoping pattern, or offer extensible term fields.

Four snags, all in the new-app frontend on-ramp: **1. Asset base resolved from `getcwd()` (breaks under the documented dev server).** `InertiaServiceProvider::register()` calls `registerWithRoot(null)`, which falls back to `getcwd()` for the Vite base (`{cwd}/public`). Under `php -S 127.0.0.1:8080 -t public`, the worker's `getcwd()` is the **docroot**, so `ViteAssetManager` looks for the manifest at `public/public/build/.vite/manifest.json`, finds nothing, and emits an **empty ``** — the page returns 200 with a blank `#app` and Vue never boots, with no error. Fix: resolve the asset base from the project root (the provider already receives `$this->projectRoot` via `setKernelContext`), not `getcwd()`. Our workaround: `chdir($projectRoot)` at the top of `public/index.php`. **2. Page payload is emitted in a ``. Stock `@inertiajs/vue3` `createInertiaApp` reads `el.dataset.page` (the attribute on the mount node) and finds nothing. We had to read the script tag and pass `page` explicitly. Either align with the Inertia `data-page` attribute convention so the stock client bootstrap works, or document this prominently. **3. `ViteAssetManager` hardcodes bundle + entry.** `RootTemplateRenderer` calls `assetTags()` with no args, fixing the dev entry to `resources/js/app.ts` and bundle `build`. An entry named `app.js` or a different output dir 404s in dev with no hint. Make bundle/entry configurable. **4. Vite `publicDir` overlaps the build target.** Building into `public/build/` while Vite's default `publicDir` is `public/` makes Vite copy `public/index.php` into the build and warn. The starter `vite.config` should set `publicDir: false`. **Suggested fix** Ship a working Inertia + Vite starter: resolve the asset base from project root; align (or document) the page-payload location; make bundle/entry configurable; and include a `vite.config` with `publicDir: false` and the expected entry path. **Dependencies / links:** Depends on NotificationDispatcher channel ownership and Mercure transport contracts; #1578 depends on this decision.

## Original report (preserved)

**Symptom**

`waaseyaa/notification` and `waaseyaa/mercure` both ship, but real-time notifications need app glue for what looks like first-party capability:

- `NotificationServiceProvider::buildChannels()` wires only `mail` + `database`. There is **no Mercure `ChannelInterface`** anywhere — `mercure` ships only `MercurePublisher` (a raw hub publish), not a notification channel.
- `NotificationDispatcher` is `final` and its channel map is injected at construction. There's no tag/hook to add a channel to the dispatcher the package already bound, so "also send over Mercure" means replacing the dispatcher binding wholesale.

**Where it bit us (Wiisnin, alpha.192)**

New-order notifications go to the vendor over Mercure (live order screen) + mail. We had to write a `MercureChannel` adapter and build our own dispatcher with the channel map:

```php
final class MercureChannel implements ChannelInterface {
    public function __construct(private MercurePublisher $publisher) {}
    public function send(NotifiableInterface $n, NotificationInterface $note): void {
        if (!method_exists($note, 'toMercure')) return;
        $topic = (string) ($n->routeNotificationFor('mercure') ?: '');
        if ($topic !== '') $this->publisher->publish($topic, $note->toMercure($n));
    }
}
```

**Suggested fix**

- Ship a first-party `MercureChannel` (wrapping `MercurePublisher`) registered under the `mercure` channel name when a hub is configured.
- Let channels be contributed into the dispatcher via a service tag / collector (or a `HasNotificationChannelsInterface`) instead of a hardcoded `buildChannels()`, so apps and packages can add channels without replacing the dispatcher.

## Current backlog disposition (2026-08-16)

**Measurable outcome:** Choose lazy policy construction or a non-fatal typed diagnostic for missing required dependencies, with a production-boot acceptance test.

**Dependencies / links:** Depends on policy discovery, container binding availability, and fail-closed access behavior.

**Why this is not ready:** The lifecycle and error-handling model is an unresolved architecture choice.

**Authority boundary:** This disposition preserves the idea; it does not authorize implementation, release, deployment, production activation, or operational mutation.

---

## Original report (preserved)

**Symptom**

The kernel discovers `#[PolicyAttribute]` access policies and instantiates them **through the container at boot**. A policy with any constructor dependency that isn't bound makes the *entire* kernel boot fail — HTTP and CLI, including unrelated commands:

```
[Waaseyaa] Boot failed: Cannot resolve constructor parameter "directory"
(type App\Access\VendorStaffDirectory) for access policy App\Access\MenuItemAccessPolicy:
the service is not bound in the kernel container. Ensure the service is registered in a
ServiceProvider::register() before kernel boot.
```

There's no per-policy degradation — one unconstructable policy takes down everything.

**Where it bit us (Wiisnin, alpha.192)**

Group-scoped policies (`VendorAccessPolicy`, `MenuItemAccessPolicy`, `OrderAccessPolicy`) share a `VendorStaffDirectory` (resolves vendor → group membership). Adding them broke `app:seed` and every request until we bound the dep in `register()`:

```php
$this->singleton(VendorStaffDirectory::class, function (): VendorStaffDirectory {
    $etm = $this->resolve(EntityTypeManager::class);
    return new VendorStaffDirectory(
        $etm->getRepository('vendor'),
        $etm->getRepository('group_membership'),
    );
});
```

The reference apps (fnpi) don't hit this because their policies are no-arg and assembled by hand via `new EntityAccessHandler([...])` — so the auto-discovery DI path is under-exercised, and the first policy that needs a dependency runs into it.

**Suggested fix**

- Resolve discovered policies lazily (construct only when a check for that entity type runs), so an app that assembles its own handler isn't forced to satisfy boot-time construction too.

## Original report (preserved)

**Symptom**

The `#[ContentEntityType(id: 'doc_chunk')]` attribute drives field discovery / metadata but is **not** what registers the type. `optimize:manifest` reports `0 attribute entity types` even with the attribute present; registration happens only because `config/entity-types.php` returns `new EntityType(id, label, class, keys)` for each. Adding a `doc_chunk` content entity attribute-first (following UPGRADING.md) didn't register it. We had to also add a matching `new EntityType(...)` row to `config/entity-types.php` before the repository and table existed.

**Suggested fix**

Either scan the app's `src/` for `#[ContentEntityType]` and auto-register (so the attribute is sufficient), or document clearly that attribute-first defines *shape* while `config/entity-types.php` (or `EntityType::fromClass()` in a provider) still does the *registration*. ## Original report (preserved)

**Symptom**

`MessagingServiceProvider` binds `ProviderInterface` to `NullLlmProvider` by default, and the framework never reads an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (Anthropic is entirely app-wired; only `OPENAI_API_KEY` is read, and only for embeddings). So a fresh app's agent runs **"succeed" but return the literal placeholder** `"[LLM unavailable in this environment …]"`. Combined with the agent run being async (dispatched to a Messenger handler, needs a worker / sync transport) and `BroadcastStorage` being unbound (#006), the shipped agent HTTP/SSE surface returns no real, streamed answer until the app binds a provider, a worker, and broadcast storage.

**Where it bit us (oiatc-waaseyaa, alpha.188)**

Tracing what `/api/ai/agent/run` does out of the box, runs came back with the placeholder text shaped like a successful response. We bound `ProviderInterface` → `AnthropicProvider(getenv('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'), model)` ourselves.

**Suggested fix**

Keep `NullLlmProvider` as the default but make it **loud** — log a `warning` once at boot when the active chat provider is Null, and/or have the agent endpoint surface a clear "no model configured" error rather than a success-shaped placeholder. Document the provider + worker + broadcast prerequisites for the agent endpoint in one place.
